related_questions.question: Where can I not conceal carry in Texas?

text_blocks.snippet: In Texas, you cannot conceal carry in several locations, including secured airport areas, schools (including colleges and universities), polling places on election days, and government courthouses. Businesses with visible signage prohibiting handguns, also known as 30.06 or 30.07 signs, are also off-limits. Additionally, businesses that derive 51% or more of their income from alcohol sales are prohibited from allowing concealed carry.

list.snippet: Secured Airport Areas: This includes areas beyond security checkpoints.
Schools and Colleges: This includes both public and private K-12 schools, as well as colleges and universities.
Polling Places: On election days, concealed carry is prohibited at polling locations.
Government Courthouses: Concealed carry is not permitted within the courthouse building.
Businesses with Signage: Businesses can prohibit concealed carry by posting specific signs (30.06 for concealed carry, 30.07 for open carry).
Alcohol-Serving Establishments: Businesses licensed by the Texas Alcoholic Beverage Commission (TABC) that earn 51% or more of their revenue from alcohol sales are off-limits for concealed carry.
Racetracks: These are also explicitly mentioned as prohibited locations.

related_questions.question: Can you shoot on your property in Texas?

text_blocks.snippet: In Texas, shooting on private property is generally legal, especially in rural areas, but there are restrictions, particularly within city limits. It's crucial to ensure safety and avoid actions that could endanger others, such as firing in a manner that could cause a bullet to cross property lines or endanger people or buildings.

list.title: Rural vs. Urban:
list.snippet: Shooting on private property is more common and generally accepted in rural areas, but cities may have stricter ordinances, even prohibiting it entirely, regardless of acreage.

list.title: Safety:
list.snippet: Regardless of location, gun owners must prioritize safety. This includes never pointing a firearm at anyone, treating every gun as if it were loaded, and avoiding firing at inappropriate targets.

list.title: Proximity to Neighbors:
list.snippet: In Texas, you generally need to be more than 150 feet from a residence or occupied building on a neighboring property when shooting.

list.title: Potential for Danger:
list.snippet: Discharging a firearm in a way that could cause a bullet to cross property lines or endanger people, vehicles, or buildings can be considered disorderly conduct.

list.title: Self-Defense:
list.snippet: Texas law allows the use of deadly force in self-defense or defense of others when facing imminent danger on your own property, but actions must be reasonable.

list.title: Castle Doctrine:
list.snippet: Texas has a "stand your ground" law, also known as the Castle Doctrine, which allows the use of deadly force to defend yourself or your property, but this doesn't give a free pass to shoot anyone trespassing.

list.title: Property Owners' Rights:
list.snippet: Private property owners can prohibit firearms on their property, requiring appropriate notice to be given.

text_blocks.snippet: In Summary: Shooting on your property in Texas is legal in many cases, but it's essential to be aware of local ordinances, practice safe gun handling, and be mindful of potential danger to others and surrounding structures.

related_questions.question: Can I buy a gun if I've been in a mental hospital in Texas?

text_blocks.snippet: In Texas, whether or not you can buy a gun after being in a mental hospital depends on the circumstances of your hospitalization. Federal law prohibits firearm possession for individuals who have been "adjudicated as a mental defective" or "committed to a mental institution". If your stay was an involuntary commitment ordered by a court or other lawful authority, you may be prohibited from owning a gun. However, if your hospitalization was voluntary or for observation only, and not a formal commitment, it may not impact your ability to purchase a firearm.

list.title: Involuntary Commitment:
list.snippet: If you were involuntarily committed to a mental health facility by a court, board, commission, or other lawful authority, you may be prohibited from owning a firearm under federal law.

list.title: Voluntary Commitment or Observation:
list.snippet: If your stay was voluntary (you checked yourself in) or you were held for a short period of observation (like a 72-hour hold) and then released, it may not affect your ability to purchase a gun.

list.title: Texas State Law:
list.snippet: Texas state law also requires reporting certain court-ordered mental health hospitalizations to the FBI for use in the National Instant Criminal Background Check System (NICS), which is used by licensed gun dealers. However, this reporting is specifically for court-ordered commitments and not for voluntary stays or observation periods.

list.title: Federal Law:
list.snippet: Under federal law, you are prohibited from possessing a firearm if you have been "adjudicated as a mental defective" or "committed to a mental institution". This includes formal commitments ordered by a court.

list.title: Exceptions:
list.snippet: There may be ways to have your firearm rights restored after a commitment, but it typically involves a legal process and potentially a hearing.

text_blocks.snippet: In conclusion: If you were involuntarily committed to a mental health facility in Texas, you should be aware that you may be prohibited from purchasing a firearm under both federal and potentially state law. However, if your hospitalization was voluntary or for observation only, it may not affect your ability to purchase a gun. You may want to consult with a legal professional or the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives (ATF) to determine the specific implications of your situation.
